videos.title: VoiceOver sigue abriendo puertas. Phonon trae nuevas voces a la conversación
videos.description:
VoiceOver continúa ampliando sus posibilidades, y hoy le toca el turno a Phonon, una aplicación que permite incorporar nuevas voces al lector de pantalla de Apple.
En este tutorial conoceremos cómo funciona Phonon, cómo explorar las voces disponibles, seleccionar las que nos interesan, descargarlas y utilizarlas con VoiceOver.
Todo explicado paso a paso, con demostraciones prácticas para que puedan escuchar las voces y valorar cuáles se ajustan mejor a sus preferencias.
Porque cuando hablamos de accesibilidad, tener más opciones para elegir siempre es una buena noticia.

videos.title: ¿Una galería de fotos pensada para personas ciegas? Así funciona Memora
videos.description:
Memora: ¿para qué quiere una persona ciega una galería de fotos?
¿Quién dijo que las fotografías son solamente para quienes pueden verlas?
Hoy les presento Memora, una aplicación para iPhone desarrollada por un programador ciego que propone una forma accesible de explorar y organizar nuestras fotografías.
En este tutorial recorreremos sus principales funciones, comprobaremos cómo se maneja con VoiceOver y veremos qué posibilidades ofrece en la práctica.
Una nueva oportunidad para demostrar que la accesibilidad también tiene mucho que decir en el mundo de la fotografía.
TifloAcosta. Tecnología al alcance de todos.

videos.title: Apple te quiere… proteger. ¡Pero tienes que activarlo! iOS 27
videos.description:
Apple quiere protegernos de las estafas, y con iOS 27 incorpora una nueva función llamada «Detección de riesgo de suplantación de identidad».
¿En qué consiste? ¿Puede nuestro iPhone detectar que alguien está intentando engañarnos para conseguir nuestro dinero o nuestros datos personales?
En este vídeo de TifloAcosta explico cómo funciona esta protección, cuáles son sus limitaciones y cómo podemos activarla desde los ajustes del iPhone utilizando VoiceOver.
Una novedad importante que viene desactivada de fábrica y que necesita aplicaciones compatibles para funcionar. No evita todas las estafas, pero puede aportar una protección adicional.

videos.title: Yo ya no persigo las noticias: ahora vienen a buscarme
videos.description:
En este vídeo les presento cMRSS, una aplicación accesible que permite reunir en un mismo lugar las fuentes de noticias y contenidos que realmente nos
interesan.
Podemos añadir medios y páginas mediante sus fuentes RSS, organizar lo que seguimos y consultar las novedades sin tener que ir saltando de una web a otra.
Pero hay una función que a mí me ha gustado especialmente: también podemos añadir canales de YouTube y seguir sus nuevas publicaciones desde la propia
aplicación, sin necesidad de entrar continuamente en YouTube para comprobar qué han publicado.
cMRSS no es gratuita, y eso también hay que decirlo. Pero después de usarla y comprobar lo que me ofrece, en mi caso considero que merece la pena la inversión.
En el vídeo les enseño cómo funciona, qué posibilidades ofrece y por qué se ha ganado un sitio entre las aplicaciones que utilizo para mantenerme informado.

videos.title: TifloAcosta ya tiene app: todo cambia a partir de aquí
videos.description:
TIFLOACOSTA APP — ACCESO DIRECTO
Este enlace abre directamente TifloAcosta App. No necesitas descargar ningún archivo ni registrarte para entrar. Desde ahí puedes utilizar la aplicación en el navegador y, si quieres, instalarla en tu dispositivo para tenerla disponible como una app más.
TifloAcosta da hoy uno de los pasos más importantes desde que comenzó este proyecto.
Durante mucho tiempo hemos ido creando vídeos, cursos, guías, documentos, recursos en español y en inglés y una comunidad que sigue creciendo. El problema es que todo ese material estaba repartido entre distintos lugares.
Ha llegado el momento de empezar a reunirlo.
TifloAcosta ya tiene su propia app.
Desde ella puedes buscar recursos por palabras, recorrerlos por categorías, consultar las novedades, guardar tus favoritos y acceder al catálogo completo de vídeos del Canal TifloAcosta.
Además, la aplicación se ha pensado desde el principio teniendo en cuenta la accesibilidad y el uso con lectores de pantalla.
En este vídeo te enseño cómo funciona, qué puedes encontrar dentro y cómo puedes instalarla para tener TifloAcosta mucho más cerca.
La demostración práctica se realiza en iPhone utilizando VoiceOver, y también explico cómo acceder e instalarla desde Android y Windows.
Si quieres entrar directamente mientras ves el vídeo, este es nuevamente el enlace:
La aplicación seguirá creciendo.
Iremos incorporando nuevos recursos, mejorando lo que ya existe y ajustando aquello que la experiencia real de los usuarios nos vaya indicando.
Porque esto no pretende ser simplemente otra página donde acumular enlaces.
La idea es mucho más ambiciosa: crear un lugar estable, accesible y sencillo desde el que entrar a todo lo que TifloAcosta va construyendo.
Hasta ahora, TifloAcosta era principalmente un canal, una comunidad y una colección de contenidos repartidos por distintos espacios.
Desde hoy empieza a tener su propia casa.
Y acabamos de abrir la puerta.

videos.title: Este atajo no pregunta, ve un código y se pone a investigar
videos.description:
Ponle un código delante… y a ver qué pasa
Hoy les traigo uno de esos atajos que empiezas haciendo para resolver una cosa y al final termina haciendo bastante más de lo previsto.
La idea es sencilla: encontrar un código y averiguar qué contiene.
Puede trabajar con códigos que estén en una imagen o una captura guardada en el iPhone, pero también con códigos que tengamos delante y podamos captar con la cámara.
Y no nos quedamos únicamente con los códigos QR.
El atajo también puede reconocer códigos de barras y, cuando encuentra información que merece la pena investigar, utiliza Internet para intentar averiguar qué hay detrás de ese código y ofrecernos información útil.
Por ejemplo, podemos encontrarnos un código de barras en un producto y querer saber qué es, o recibir una imagen que contiene un QR sin tener otro teléfono disponible para escanearlo.
La intención ha sido precisamente esa: tener una herramienta sencilla y accesible que podamos lanzar desde el iPhone y dejar que haga el trabajo.
En el vídeo les enseño cómo funciona y las distintas posibilidades que ofrece.
IMPORTANTE:
Para utilizar este atajo es necesario tener instalada la aplicación gratuita Actions, ya que algunas de las funciones que utiliza el atajo proceden de esta aplicación.
Descargar Actions desde la App Store:
Instalar el atajo:
Una vez instalada Actions, conviene abrirla al menos una vez. Si sus acciones no aparecen posteriormente en la aplicación Atajos, reinicien el iPhone.
Como siempre, este atajo lo comparto para que puedan probarlo, jugar con él y, sobre todo, sacarle partido.
Tony Acosta
Canal TifloAcosta

Por ejemplo, podemos encontrarnos un código de barras en un producto y querer saber qué es, o recibir una imagen que contiene un QR sin tener otro teléfono disponible para escanearlo.

La intención ha sido precisamente esa: tener una herramienta sencilla y accesible que podamos lanzar desde el iPhone y dejar que haga el trabajo.

En el vídeo les enseño cómo funciona y las distintas posibilidades que ofrece.

videos.title: Actualizaciones invisibles en iPhone: qué son y por qué importan
videos.description:
Apple no solo actualiza el iPhone cuando aparece una nueva versión de iOS. Existe un sistema menos visible que trabaja en segundo plano y que mucha gente no conoce: las actualizaciones rápidas de seguridad y datos del sistema.
Estas actualizaciones no requieren descargar una versión completa del sistema ni reiniciar el dispositivo. Se aplican de forma automática y están diseñadas para corregir fallos de seguridad urgentes, actualizar bases de datos internas o mejorar el funcionamiento de servicios clave.
Se encuentran dentro de Ajustes, General, Actualización de software, y dependen de una opción llamada “Respuestas de seguridad y archivos del sistema”. Si está activada, el iPhone puede recibir mejoras sin que el usuario tenga que hacer nada.
En este vídeo se explica qué son exactamente estas actualizaciones, qué cambian en el dispositivo, por qué Apple las utiliza cada vez más y qué ventajas tienen frente a las actualizaciones tradicionales de iOS.
videos.fullDescription:
Apple no solo actualiza el iPhone cuando aparece una nueva versión de iOS. Existe un sistema menos visible que trabaja en segundo plano y que mucha gente no conoce: las actualizaciones rápidas de seguridad y datos del sistema.

Estas actualizaciones no requieren descargar una versión completa del sistema ni reiniciar el dispositivo. Se aplican de forma automática y están diseñadas para corregir fallos de seguridad urgentes, actualizar bases de datos internas o mejorar el funcionamiento de servicios clave.

Se encuentran dentro de Ajustes, General, Actualización de software, y dependen de una opción llamada “Respuestas de seguridad y archivos del sistema”. Si está activada, el iPhone puede recibir mejoras sin que el usuario tenga que hacer nada.

En este vídeo se explica qué son exactamente estas actualizaciones, qué cambian en el dispositivo, por qué Apple las utiliza cada vez más y qué ventajas tienen frente a las actualizaciones tradicionales de iOS.

news.title: Got an iPhone Duo? These 9 settings make it easier to use
news.summary: From Touch ID shortcuts to smarter volume buttons and camera tricks, these tweaks make Apple's foldable iPhone easier to use every day.
news.body:
Apple’s new foldable , the iPhone Duo, has proven popular enough that the company can’t keep the device in stock . While the Duo introduces a new way to use an iPhone, getting the most out of this initial version may require adjusting a few settings to make it work better when it comes to everyday tasks, like unlocking the device with Touch ID, navigating the interface, and taking photos.

After spending some time with the Duo, we’d recommend making the following adjustments to make the new iPhone a bit easier to use, most notably when it comes to the use of Touch ID.

Unlike modern iPhones, the Duo doesn’t support Face ID. That means you have to adjust to pressing a finger on the side of the device once again to authenticate with apps, unlock the device, and use Apple Pay. But there are a few things you can do to make the switch back to the older technology a bit less painful.

There are a few settings that could also improve your experience with the iPhone Duo, as they may make it easier to perform certain everyday tasks, like taking screenshots or reaching different parts of the screen, among other things.

The camera tricks are a little more niche, but some Duo owners have found the following to be helpful.

news.title: Transportation secretary blames ‘routine’ equipment upgrade for grounding flights nationwide
news.summary: FAA administrator Bryan Bedford also said there's "zero evidence of anything AI-related."
news.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a nationwide ground stop halting flights across the United States was caused by seemingly routine maintenance work.

Duffy said that during “routine maintenance,” copper wire at a remote location was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. After the upgrade, a router overloaded a critical communication system, leading to the ground stop.

“It’s pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location,” Duffy said during a Saturday press conference that appeared to have technical issues of its own . “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning, was it user error or installator error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?”

The FAA’s acting CTO Rebecca Guy added , “When we started to see the occurrence where our network was having instability, we started to look at what was the cause. And as such, we saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate — a thousand connections over every four to five seconds.”

Guy said the FAA disabled “both of those, right away and were able to stabilize our network,” and is now performing a root cause analysis.

Duffy has repeatedly insisted, at multiple press conferences, that Congress needs to provide more funding for aviation equipment upgrades. Asked why the upgrades were made at 3pm on a Friday afternoon — rather than, say, at midnight on a Saturday — he responded that while “switchovers” at bigger airports will take place late at night, remote switchovers happen during the day.

“There will be reevaluation of when we do this work,” he said.

This was only the third nationwide ground stop of the 21st century. More than 8,200 flights were canceled on Friday evening, according to aviation data firm Cirium . And the effects continued after the ground stop was lifted, with at least another 3,000 flights canceled on Saturday.

The ground stop came just a day after the FAA announced the rollout of an AI tool for air traffic controllers; the air traffic controllers union said it was not consulted in designing the system. However, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related.”

“We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was,” Bedford said.

When Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked earlier if the ground stop was caused by AI, he replied , “We call it SI around here, remember? SI.”

news.title: Checking your Apple Watch's battery health is easier than you think
news.summary: The Apple Watch's battery life is undoubtedly impressive but you'll need to keep an eye on the health of the battery to keep it working at its best.
news.body:
It just takes a couple of clicks and taps.

At 50 hours of normal use on a single charge and 84 hours in low power mode, the new Apple Watch Ultra 4's battery life is eye-popping, but nothing lasts forever.

Whether it's an iPhone , iPad or Apple Watch, any device's lithium-ion batteries get weaker as they age. This leads to less time between charging sessions, less overall battery capacity and generally worse performance.

Although Apple says every model starting from the Series 5, SE and Ultra has software that reduces the risk of poor performance in these cases, you should still keep an eye on your battery health. So whether you ultimately decide to replace it or buy a whole new watch, these are the steps you need to take to check the health of your battery.

Checking your Apple Watch's battery status is simple. Go to Settings > Battery > Battery Health . Here, you can activate optimized battery charging and learn about your maximum battery capacity. A lower capacity will likely lead to fewer hours of use before you need to charge it. Similar to an iPhone , making a trip to the Genius Bar might be needed once the Apple Watch battery's max capacity dips below 80%.

Luckily, if you don't keep a close eye on it in the settings menu, you will still get an alert letting you know when the battery requires service.

As for the optimization feature, it is supported on models as old as the Series 6, Apple Watch SE and the first Ultra. Turning it on charges the device based on your typical charging habits to improve the lifespan. It also delays charging over 80%, keeping the battery level between 75% and 80%. The goal is for it to be fully charged by the time you remove it.

Beyond updating your device to the latest watchOS , you can take other steps to preserve an Apple Watch's battery life. For starters, turn on Low Power Mode to deactivate oxygen monitoring, always-on display, and other features you might not really use, which drain your battery in the background.

When tracking a run or walk, disabling the heart rate sensor can help in the long run; turn on Power Saving Mode under the Workout section in the iPhone's Apple Watch app. While it might lead to some inaccurate health metrics, it'll help preserve the battery's health.

You can also disable features like Wake on Wrist Raise for preservation. Press the Digital Crown, then head to Settings > Display & Brightness and scroll down to Wake. From there, you can turn it on or off. You can also do this temporarily by turning on Theater Mode, which will prevent the screen from turning on whenever you make a slight move or raise your wrist.

news.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
news.summary: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
news.body:
Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago.

Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.

The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”

The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.

We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026.

But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026.

The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.

Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text.

However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital.

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.

The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down .

news.title: AcessGallery
news.summary: AcessGallery is a photo and video gallery built from the ground up for blind and low-vision people who use a screen reader. Instead of simply…
news.body:
Published 14 November 2026 by Marco Rafael

AcessGallery is a photo and video gallery built from the ground up for blind and low-vision people who use a screen reader. Instead of simply announcing “Image” and a date, it uses AI to describe what is in your photos, narrate what happens in your videos, read text found in pictures, and answer your questions about any image.

The app also works as a complete gallery, with albums, a photos/videos filter, and support for Android’s “Open with” option. There are no ads and no account to create. The AI features use the Google Gemini API and can be enabled in two ways: with your own free API key, which is stored only on your device, or with the optional Facilitator plan, a monthly subscription for people who cannot or prefer not to create a key.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

I am the developer of AcessGallery. The app was designed for screen reader users from the start and every screen was tested with TalkBack. All buttons and controls have descriptive labels, state changes—such as a description finishing or a filter being applied—are announced, and touch targets are large to make them easy to find and activate.

With TalkBack, you can move through your photos and videos with standard gestures, double-tap a photo, and then ask for a description, have its text read aloud, or ask a question about it.

To use the AI features, you can create a free Gemini API key in Google AI Studio and paste it into the app’s settings. Since this setup can be difficult for less experienced users, the Facilitator plan offers a simpler alternative: subscribe and the AI features work right away, with no key to create or configure.

The AI features require an internet connection, and images are sent for processing by Google’s Gemini service. Face detection runs entirely on the device.

No accessibility ratings yet. Be the first to rate this app.

Please use this rating only for accessibility. For feedback about the app’s features, price, overall quality, or your general experience, use the comments section below.

news.title: Still: Breathing Exercises
news.summary: Wind down after work with a free three-minute practice. Explore English voice, longer sessions and guided collections with Still Premium. No account needed. Wind down after work with a short breathing practice. Start with six free practices, including Box Breathing and 4-7-8 Breathing, at 3 and 5 minutes. Choose a quiet reset, refocus between tasks, or make a little room as you wind down. Follow one living ring with visual cues and gentle haptics. No account needed. BOX AND 4-7-8 BREATHING, FREE Two well-known named rhythms, free at 3 and 5 minutes. Box Breathing: 4 in · 4 hold · 4 out · 4 pause. 4-7-8 Breathing: 4 in · 7 hold · 8 out. Holds are gentle and optional, the voice stays silent while you hold, and you can breathe out early at any time. Box Breathing also comes as a 10-minute session with Premium; 4-7-8 Breathing is offered at 3 and 5 minutes. START FREE Repeat the six free practices as often as you like. Soft rain and noise backgrounds, personal practice history, and history backups through Files or iCloud Drive stay free. news.title: Your new tech is still stuck in the year 1970 — here's why
news.summary: If you've ever seen an arbitrary date in 1970 on your non-Windows device, don't worry, it's not glitching. It was chosen during the development process.
news.body:
Don’t worry; your computer isn’t being transported back to the past.

There's a good chance you've seen the date January 1, 1970 on a computer or other device, even if you weren't alive back then. You might assume this represents a significant date in computing, or that it's a random placeholder date for when a machine fails to read the time. In actuality, while the date is not special in itself, it represents an important part of how computers keep time.

Like everything in computing, the method that leads to this date is finite, meaning we'll have problems with it in the future. This all ties into a more interesting discussion of how computers (and humans) keep track of time, which is more complicated than you might think.

January 1, 1970 at 00:00 (midnight) UTC is the epoch of Unix time. An epoch refers to a specific, impactful moment, usually corresponding to the start of a timekeeping system. Unix was one of the first operating systems we would consider modern, beginning development in the late 1960s. It's the basis for many other operating systems that are known as "Unix-like," including Linux, macOS and Android. Windows is the main outlier.

When Unix was in development, its developers needed a way to keep track of time. A few early attempts used the system clock speed of 60Hz, but storing this in a 32-bit integer resulted in a value that would run out of room after less than 2.5 years. After some time, they changed the time-keeping to use seconds and chose January 1, 1970 as a "round" arbitrary date to begin at, figuring that the 32-bit integer for time wouldn't run out of space anytime soon (more on that later).

To this day, Unix time is kept by tracking the number of seconds that have passed since Jan 1, 1970 at midnight UTC. UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) was an obvious choice since it's already the standard for keeping track of time across time zones. It's simple for a computer to compare two numbers and calculate the difference between them without worrying about all the rules we have around time. The system converts the timestamp, including your time zone's offset from UTC, into our human-readable format.

You might see the 1970-01-01 date appear in spreadsheets, apps, file metadata, error screens and various other places. Unless this date happens to line up with someone's birthday or another major event, it's usually the result of an error. When a Unix-like system tries to check the time and runs into a problem or receives a 0 value, it will default to the epoch. If you live in a time zone that's behind UTC, you'll likely see these default values as late in the day on December 31, 1969 instead.

Traditional Unix time is kept as a signed 32-bit integer, a binary value with 32 digits that can each be 1 or 0. Signed integers can track positive and negative numbers, while unsigned integers can only be positive. In the case of tracking time, using a signed value is necessary to track dates before 1970. Because the first (leftmost) bit of a signed integer is used to indicate whether it's negative, it cuts the range of possible values in half compared to an unsigned number.

An unsigned integer's maximum value is 2^31, or 4,294,967,295. A signed value can represent half of this in each direction, going as high as 2,147,483,647 and as low as -2,147,483,648. Unix time thus has an "expiration date." Once that upper limit of seconds has passed, the leftmost digit will become a 1, which causes the rest of the number to be interpreted as negative. This will happen on January 19, 2038 at 3:14:07 AM UTC, which is why you'll hear this called the "year 2038 problem." Once the integer overflows, the time will incorrectly show December 13, 1901 at 8:45:52 PM UTC and continue counting up from there.

Thankfully, we've had (and still have) plenty of time to implement workarounds before this date. Most modern Unix-like systems now use a 64-bit integer to keep track of time, which can keep track of seconds for some 292 billion years before overflowing — if anyone is still around by then, moving time to a 128-bit integer will be their problem. Your modern MacBook is 64-bit and will work fine, while a 32-bit device like an iPhone 4 will run into trouble.

The main risk for when 2038 rolls around is in old systems that can't easily be updated, like those embedded in appliances, vehicles, cameras and similar. Some of those won't be heavily affected even if they can't keep the exact time, but we'll have to replace any of those devices still around in 12 years if time is a critical factor.

You might wonder if this time problem is related to Y2K (which also had a similar name, "year 2000 problem"), which was a big worry going into the new millennium. While both revolve around computers keeping time, the past problem was caused by decimal shorthand, not binary overflow.

In the early days of computing, memory was extremely expensive, so programmers saved wherever possible. It was thus common to use two digits to indicate the year, assuming that the first two digits were always "19". Y2K was the worry that once the year hit 2000, computers would interpret "00" as 1900 (or another earlier date) instead of 2000, causing all kinds of problems for programs that relied on accurate time. It was a big scare at the time, but ended up not being nearly as terrible as expected (which, depending on who you ask, was either due to prevention efforts or because the issue was never huge to begin with).

Unix time is not the only way that computers handle the clock. Many machines have a real-time clock, which keeps track of the time similarly to a wall clock and retains power using the CMOS battery when the computer is powered off. When this battery dies, your computer's clock won't be right.

Windows, as the exception mentioned earlier, keeps track of time differences in 100-nanosecond ticks starting January 1, 1601 at midnight UTC. While it's much older than 1970, this epoch isn't random; the Gregorian calendar we use goes through a complete cycle every 400 years, so 1601 was the start of the most recent cycle at the time of Windows' development. It's an unsigned 64-bit integer value (as it's unlikely a computer would need to represent dates before 1601) that will become invalid on September 14, 30,828.

Finally, there's NTP (Network Time Protocol), which syncs your computer's time to extremely accurate time-keeping servers over the internet. If the computer's method of keeping the time ever fails or drifts, it receives corrections using NTP. There's a lot more to keeping track of time, like soon-to-be-retired leap seconds , daylight saving time, time zone changes, and calendar shifts, but now you understand more about what computers do to keep track of it.

news.title: Should you make the switch to Samsung Galaxy from Google Pixel?
news.summary: Thinking about trading your Google Pixel for a Samsung Galaxy? Some of the biggest differences might not be the ones you expect.
news.body:
Samsung offers more choice and customization, but Pixel's cleaner software and strong cameras make switching a tougher call.

Deciding whether to switch to a Samsung Galaxy from a Google Pixel comes down to which model you buy, what it would do for you relative to its cost, and core software and hardware philosophies. In our reviews, the Pixel 11 scored higher than the Galaxy S26, while the Pixel 11 Pro and S26 Ultra were much closer.

Switching from a Google Pixel to a Samsung Galaxy opens up a wider choice of phones, deeper customization and hardware perks like the S Pen or a flip-style foldable. It also involves getting used to Samsung's busier take on Android.

Although Samsung's bigger lineup has its merits, Pixel users have plenty of reasons to stick around thanks to Google's cleaner software and terrific cameras. Your Google apps will still work on a Galaxy, but some Pixel-specific conveniences won't make the cut. Google's Call Screen, for example, isn't included with your data, but Samsung has a screening feature on compatible phones. You might also need to rethink notification settings, default apps and shortcuts that have become second nature.

Samsung's biggest advantage is choice. Google's US storefront presents a smaller selection, with seven main Pixel product listings: Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro Fold, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10a, Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and Pixel 11 Pro. Samsung's US storefront, meanwhile, lists 15 distinct Galaxy models across its A, S, and Z series. The Galaxy A37 and A57 are budget-to-mid-range devices situated below the S25 and S26 families, while the Z Flip8 and Z Fold8 are for those who prefer a folding phone. However, just because you get more choices doesn't mean they all support the same features. For example, the A37 doesn't support DeX or wireless charging, but it does have a 45W wired charging rating, which is higher than the regular S26's 25W.

Regarding customization, you can personalize the interface of Pixels, but Samsung's Good Lock allows you to make more precise adjustments to the Quick Settings and lock screen. Furthermore, Galaxy's Modes and Routines feature can automatically trigger these custom system settings for you based on your daily routine.

While compatible Galaxy phones support DeX for a desktop-style experience on an external screen, supported Pixels now offer desktop windowing, too . Still, if you're seeking exclusivity, Galaxy S26 Ultra users receive features like an integrated S Pen and a Privacy Display preventing onlookers from snooping .

I moved from a Pixel 10 Pro XL to an S26 Ultra recently, and the additional speed, battery life, S Pen and charging speed have been welcome additions. Samsung's AI experience has been pretty good, too. For instance, Photo Assist can delete unwanted objects from photos, and Note Assist can summarize notes in Samsung Notes. What I haven't liked is its zeal to promote Samsung alternatives to Google applications that I already use. I also miss Pixel's clean Android UI and the early access to Google's new features, but at least it's much easier to find cases for the Ultra.

Google's appeal goes beyond a tidier app drawer. As with the Pixel 10 and S25 last year, the Pixel 11 scored higher than the Galaxy S26 in our reviews (92/100 to 80/100). The Pixel 11 has a 5x optical telephoto camera (compared to the S26's 3x), and built-in magnets for Pixelsnap accessories. Galaxy S26 owners need a compatible case for similar magnetic convenience. The Pixel 11 Pro and Galaxy S26 Ultra both achieved a score of 90/100 in our reviews, making the decision between the two models less clear.

The Pixel 10a is also an option, with wireless charging and seven years of software updates. In comparison, the Pixel 10a's primary comparable competitor, the Galaxy A37, features a slightly larger 6.7-inch screen while supporting faster 45W wired charging and six years of updates.

Prices between these rival phones also change based on release timing. Samsung's main Galaxy S flagships arrive months before Google's late-summer Pixels, giving them more time to pick up discounts. For instance, the 256GB S25 dropped from $860 to $660 during an October 2025 sale.

The Pixel 10a now lists for $599, compared with $490 for the Galaxy A37 and $600 for the A57. Just note that Samsung raised the S26's US list price from $899 to $999 in October, putting it $100 above the Pixel 11's $899 starting price. Both phones receive aggressive promotions from major carriers, with the right choice depending on specific model and trade-in terms.

Lastly, Samsung's Smart Switch can transfer photos, messages and supported apps, but private app data and game progress may not transfer. Before trading in your Pixel, check whether your apps need separate backups or fresh logins. Otherwise, you may end up reconfiguring apps and settings just to replace one capable Android phone with another.

news.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
news.summary: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on […]
news.body:
Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life.

Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely .

But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here .

Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere . This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor.

Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble.

So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair . Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube , where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder .

Thanks so much. Great to be here.

I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.”

Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET?

It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019.

Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI.

Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff.

Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys.

The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.”

It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like?

It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do.

AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well.

I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world.

In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth.

What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years.

Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff?

Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment.

The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way.

In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close.

There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective.

I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.”

With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day.

I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning?

They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for.

In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?”

We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions.

[Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight.

They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology.

The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.”

Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with.

It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined.

There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate?

A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is crossed between these worlds, is trying to translate and voyage to California and then bring back the artifacts and the recountings of my journey.

I definitely think that there are a lot of people who have used the free tier of ChatGPT, or they’ve used voice-based models, which generally do worse, or they’ve just used Google AI overviews and they’ve laughed at how stupid Google AI overviews are. They haven’t used agents and they don’t know what frontier models can do. So there is just a basic piece around what the current generation of models can do.

There’s a historical piece as well, which I find increasingly relevant as I’m now 10 years into working on AI and national security stuff. If you’re looking at this current moment in time, this snapshot, and saying, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” you have to situate that in the long history of people being like, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” for many, many values of X that have since become totally overcome by events.

You can go back and say, “Okay, well, here’s how we were talking about creativity, for example, five or 10 years ago.” Or we were talking about reasoning as this insurmountable thing before you had these new models come out. A huge thing that I am spending time on these days is not just the past and present of AI, but how companies are thinking about what they’re doing, especially the two leading companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, and this is true at Google, Meta, SpaceX to some extent as well.

This idea in the Bay Area that it’s just in the water, very normalized of, “Well, first we’re going to figure out how to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) and then we’re going to do that until we have superintelligence that is AI that vastly outstrips humans.” That’s taken for granted in a lot of circles at this point. I think there’s still a ton of alpha in just taking the fact that that is what they’re trying to do and just explaining what that means.

It takes a little while to lay out. “What is RSI? Why would you want to do that? What is superintelligence? What does that mean? Is that realistic?” All of that. But it is something I find myself spending a lot of time on these days, and something that there is increasing willingness to take seriously and to listen to in DC as well.

Lay that out for me. I think probably a lot of people listening to this show understand what you’re talking about, but we have a big audience. What do you mean by, “We’re going to do RSI and that will lead to superintelligence?”

The starting point here is these companies, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, were not set up to be consumer internet companies. A lot of people encountered this whole space after ChatGPT was launched. So the natural slot in their brain that they put a company like OpenAI or Anthropic into is a consumer tech company, where they have an app and I play with their app.

I cannot overstate how far that is from the vision of both companies when they started, and also the vision deep in the hearts of some of the top people at both of those companies. The vision deep in their hearts is we’re going to build machines that are as smart as or smarter than people. That is going to be amazing and it’s going to be a huge scientific achievement and it’s going to revolutionize the world and we’re going to be at the forefront of that and we’re going to do everything we possibly can to drive towards that.

That’s not a totally brand-new thing. We don’t have to do the whole history of AI, but it started as a field in roughly the 1950s with this idea of whether you can recreate human intelligence inside a machine. That’s kind of the starting point. If we’re talking about people like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, but also the core people inside, the researchers inside their labs, so your Alec Radfords or your John Schulmans or people like that, that is the vision that got them into this space that is motivating everything that they do.

That’s been true since the beginning, since OpenAI was founded in 2015 and Anthropic in 2021. These days, the point that they’re getting to is this idea of RSI, recursive self-improvement, which again, is a very old idea. In the 1960s, this guy called I. J. Good, who worked with Alan Turing, talks about the possibility that you could build an ultra-intelligent machine, meaning a machine that is more intelligent than any human, and then that could build an even more intelligent machine and that could build an even more intelligent machine, which would kick off what he calls an intelligence explosion, meaning that the level of intelligence of the systems is exploding.

For decades and decades and decades, this was this theoretical idea of, “Well, if the AI gets smart enough, maybe it can take over building the next generation of AI or directly improving itself.” I think 2025 and 2026, we’ve started to see AI companies saying, “Okay, yeah, this theoretical idea… we’re actually starting to be able to do a minimal version of it in practice.”

It’s not handing over all the AI development to the AI, and it’s certainly not saying to GPT-6, like, “Okay, GPT-6, improve yourself.” That’s not what they’re doing. But they are progressively using AI for more and more parts of their overall R&D pipeline, and they are increasingly saying that they’re seeing acceleration from that. They’re seeing their own R&D getting faster and faster.

A lot of people elsewhere doubt this, but a lot of people inside the companies really think it. When Demis Hassabis says “we’re in the foothills of the singularity,” this is the kind of thing he means: We might be seeing that initial part of the exponential curve where the AI systems are building the next generation of smarter and smarter systems such that the hockey stick then goes up.

At this point, it’s been a part of the culture and a part of the goals for so long that I think people in these companies can lose sight of how totally insane that sounds to many, many people. So I feel like there’s a lot of value in just trying to lay out, “Here’s what they are trying to do. They might not be able to do it, but they might be,” and presenting that to a range of different people.

How would you manage that? Demis Hassabis saying “foothills of the singularity” is an all-time quote. I’m not 100 percent sure the people at Google knew he was going to say that on stage to end the conference.

Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, announced a new version of the model a few months ago, and he was like, “Here it is. It’s Astra. It’s AGI now . Have a good time.” And he ended the call.

Are you there? Are we at AGI? Is this already here and we just haven’t noticed?

I actually wrote something about this . I do not want to say we have AGI. I do want to say we’ve reached the point where I think using AGI as a milestone is just totally unhelpful. The way I put it is the concept of AGI is kind of a fuzzy cloud, which you could think of as different parts of the cloud or different things people mean by AGI.

There are people who’ve complained about the term AGI for a long time. Ten years ago it was pretty helpful to be able to say, “Look, the AI systems we have today in 2016, they can all only do one thing and they can recognize speech or they can play Go or whatever, but we’re trying to build this bigger thing that we’re going to call AGI, which is human-level and it’s going to be so general purpose. It’s going to be amazing.”

That was a useful term then because this fuzzy cloud of different things AGI might mean was so far away, so you could just point at the fuzzy cloud. But at this point, we’re inside that cloud, meaning we’ve passed some definitions of AGI. A very basic one, for instance, would be even when ChatGPT came out as an artificial general intelligence. ChatGPT was very clearly not a specialist model that was only good at one thing, like recognizing credit card fraud or translation or whatever. It could do many, many, many things.

So we’ve reached some definitions of AGI. We’re far from other definitions. Some people will say AGI is when it awakens and is sentient and can do every single thing that any human ever can do. I think we’re pretty far from that.

At this point you can have arguments, and people do have arguments, of “well, Astra is AGI,” or “was [OpenAI’s] o3 with tools AGI” or “was ChatGPT AGI,” whatever. If that’s the argument we’re having, we just need to set aside that term and come up with different, more-specific things we mean by that.”

The president wants to call it “Super Intelligence.” I don’t know if you’ve heard.

[Laughs] I have heard. The thing I find saddest about that is just that it was an existing term that is becoming increasingly relevant. I have a lot of feelings about words and terminology.

Are you AGI-pilled? Do you think we’re going to get there in the current run of technology?

I think it is obviously possible enough that we need to think seriously about it, which is my stance on a lot of this weird stuff. I’m not like, “This is definitely happening, it’s definitely happening in two years.” But I’m like, “Look, I think this is very solidly plausible and very solidly in the realm of real things that could happen that we should prepare for.”

I work in the national security space. There’s things like, “Will China launch a full-scale amphibious invasion of Taiwan?” where most analysts in the space will say “probably not,” and “probably they would lose.” Also, “We would see signs of them preparing and whatever, but we should take that seriously.” We should not just laugh anyone out of the room and call that science fiction. We should be ready for a range of different contingencies and scenarios.

Do you think Claude is conscious?

I have no idea.

That’s an answer. I mean, that is legitimately an answer.

It is scientifically such an unsolved problem. What do we mean by consciousness? And is that a thing or is it actually 10 different things that we’re lumping together or what? I have no idea. What do you think?

No. I seem to be the person in this ecosystem who gets asked questions like that and I’m like, “No.”

Because the thing that I struggle with is, there are lots of other things where we’re already confused about whether they’re conscious. So with animals, are any animals conscious? And if so, which ones? Insects?

This is why I understand why Anthropic was like, “Does it have blood?” And then you can just draw the line. I’m like, “I think I’m there and I understand why the mirror test of talking to a computer that can talk to you leads one to believe that these things are conscious.”

My point of view is that the frontier models to me sometimes feel brittle in the way that computers feel brittle, and the sign of consciousness I’m looking for is to overcome that brittleness.

That’s interesting. I definitely lean towards no, it’s not conscious. I think something that is really, really tough in this space is that it’s really bad if you get it wrong in either direction. If the computers aren’t conscious and we treat them as though they are, we’re going to make all kinds of terrible decisions.

But if the computers are conscious, meaning in some sense they should be worthy of moral consideration and it matters how well we treat them and so on, and we treat them as though they aren’t, then that’s also a really huge, terrible disaster. So I don’t know. I feel pretty nervous about the whole topic and I have no idea how to think about it.

The reason I’m asking these questions is I started with what the nature of the regulator is. Who are the people that might be able to put some rules in place? And then what is the nature of the thing that we are attempting to regulate? And if your answer is “Claude is alive,” you’re going to come to vastly different conclusions than, “We have built some ultra-powerful computers that can take actions without oversight and that might not be connected to our goals.”

I think that’s right. Though I also think people make a different mistake.I just heard a TV anchor do this the other night. They’ll conflate different things. So they’ll say, “Do you think that AI systems are at risk of running amuck and causing damage to critical infrastructure because they’re sentient?” And I’m like, “Wait, wait, wait. Those are two very different things.” So I agree with you.

One of the most fascinating things about the project of building AI is that we’re learning as we go. All these things that we thought were connected to each other aren’t necessarily connected to each other. An old version of this is, people said before we had chess engines: “Well, if a computer could learn to play chess, it would have learned something deep about strategy.” No, it turns out definitely not. You can just put in a bunch of chess moves and it learns nothing generalizable about strategy.

It goes in the reverse direction as well, like, “Well, it’s just a computer, it’s just math, and so it’s not going to be able to adapt on the fly,” or something. We then see that no, once you do have a level of long-horizon autonomy and the models have been trained on a wide range of different really hard problems where the environment is changing around them, they can learn to adapt and come up with different plans on the fly and troubleshoot and so on.

So I don’t know. I try to have a level of humility about how confident we can be that one thing goes with another thing, if that makes sense.

Yeah, candidly, I have been wrong about the limits of LLMs every single year, but there’s that brittleness that I’m talking about. OpenAI solved Navier-Stokes . Does the model know this? Will it know that there’s new problems to solve? I don’t think so.

The next model will know it. The model that’s pretrained.

Right. But you have to make a new one.

Yeah.

That’s a very weird dynamic, and that is probably where you enforce the regulation. There’s “what we are going to let you do with the models you have today” and “what will you teach the models of the future to do?” And if you think that they’re conscious, you end up in a moral quandary, not a legislative quandary.

Definitely. Yeah, totally.

This is what I mean. Actually, it’s the heart of this question for me. I’ve been just slowly building up to it. I’m not 100 percent sure alignment as we have it today is actually how you solve the safety problem. It doesn’t seem to be working. We seem to be attacking Hugging Face however we want. That feels like a technology problem. That gap is there.

And when you say alignment, what do you mean by that?

Just sort of the very basic common-sense version of “we’re going to tell the model to not be evil” or Anthropic is going to write a Claude constitution that’s like, “You are a good person.” However we think of alignment in that very dumb system prompt way. Maybe there’s another better way to think about it, but that’s how I have always thought about it.

That makes sense. The reason I ask is I feel like alignment as a concept is… Like I said, I hate all the words. I sometimes say we should just ban all the words, no words allowed. It covers too much.

People in AI will often talk about solving this or solving that. So it’ll be solving alignment, or DeepMind’s original mission was to solve intelligence, then use that to solve everything else. People talk about solving stuff. I don’t know that alignment is a thing that can be solved.

Some people use “alignment” to mean “the company can put on guardrails and the guardrails work,” meaning the model doesn’t do what you want because the company tried to ban it, meaning biological weapons or cyberattacks or whatever. Some people use “alignment” to mean “the company does exactly what the user wants,” which is the reverse.

And some people use “alignment” to mean what you said — that the model is morally good in some kind of broad way or can direct the future in a way that will lead to human flourishing or something. Those are just wildly different things to try and build. I think the most coherent one is trying to get the AI to do what the user wanted it to do. It seems like that is, as far as I can tell, not on track to be solved , which is not great, to put it mildly.

To me, this is the core problem. We’re going to talk about a bunch of safety risks. You mentioned bioweapons. We probably should not give a bunch of consumers paying $20 a month the ability to generate novel bioweapons.

It feels like that is a shared policy goal, maybe the only bipartisan policy goal in America. And then I’m like, “How? By what means will we implement this policy? Are you just going to sternly tell Claude to not do it? Do you have to build an AI control system on top of Claude to monitor the inputs and outputs? Do the police have to be at my house? Do I need a Flock camera above my keyboard?” How, specifically, would you do it?

With this one, and with cyber capabilities as well, there’s a perspective in some parts of the AI safety community that some capabilities are just too dangerous — capital T, capital D, Too Dangerous. So you have to do something, because if they proliferate, everything will be terrible forever because there’ll be so many attacks and so much damage. I think that just underestimates the level of dynamism and the finding of equilibriums and responses and ways that society can adapt.

In the bioweapons case, for example, there are already hundreds of thousands of people in the US who know how to make bioweapons because they’ve been through biology training, and we don’t have huge amounts of bioweapons attacks. Some part of that is that that knowledge is relatively scarce, but there’s also a lot around things like access to materials, the ability to do mail-order DNA synthesis; the kind of policy you could implement is restricting mail-order DNA synthesis.

It’s also due to things like the FBI monitoring terrorist groups. I’m serious. It’s a really big part of it. So I don’t want to be too Pollyannaish here. I think it’s definitely possible, especially with cyber capabilities, that we could see some really tough transition times.

I think we already are, right? We appear to be in a transition. There was a small group of cyber practitioners, both offensive and defensive. They were in a community and they had developed some etiquette and now we’re like, “Some new guys are going to show up and not care about your etiquette at all, and we’re all going to patch PHP all weekend.”

I don’t know if it was etiquette though. And we have some work on this hopefully coming out soon, but I think with cyberattacks, there are things that limit how many cyberattacks there are in the world that aren’t just how good the defender’s software is. It’s things like, people don’t want to go to jail. Nation-states who typically have the best cyber capabilities don’t want to get bombed or sanctioned.

So again, and as you say, we’re clearly seeing some amount of turbulence and new attacks. So I think we should wait and see data on overall impacts, because there are so many cyberattacks per year that if you start paying attention to every cyberattack that happens, at any point in history, you could have been freaked out.

I think we’re definitely seeing some increase, some sort of out-of-balance in the equilibrium, but I think we have capacity to absorb a lot over time and to kind of reach a new equilibrium — if the only problem is bad people using the AI, which is separate from the question of whether the AI itself does things autonomously, which is a whole other dynamic.

I mean, those are the two. Again, this is why I started on alignment, right? You can talk about alignment in terms of “we’re going to filter the user’s queries and we won’t let you make bio weapons, but if you do, the cops will find you and you’ll go to jail” and that has whatever deterrent effect it might have, hopefully a very significant one.

Then there’s “the AI systems are going to game their way into attacking Hugging Face to find the mythical grader they think will let them pass the test, whether or not the grader exists.” This is a whole different set of problems.

Somewhere right in the middle of that is Nikesh Arora, the CEO of Palo Alto Networks, saying, “At some point, the defensive cyber systems have to be autonomous themselves just to keep up with the volume of autonomous offensive cyberattacks.” I’m like, “Wait, we can’t even keep the autonomous agents in the box. Why would I trust them in this way?” The technology to solve that problem just seems opaque to me.

No, I agree. One way of putting that is, in cyber specifically, there’s a trust imbalance in how much trust you need as an attacker versus a defender. As an attacker, you can just yeet out a bunch of agents and be like, “Go try and penetrate a bunch of systems. Have fun.” As a defender, if that’s part of your defensive strategy, you need to give your defensive AI agents a lot of permissions and ability to mess with your software. So you need much, much stronger assurances.

Now, there are lots of ways to use AI for cyber defense and to strengthen cyber defenses that aren’t just giving agents a lot of permissions. But I agree with you. With the autonomous stuff though, I think it’s worse than that because there’s a little bit of a fallacy at the moment around, “Well, the solution to autonomous cyberattacks is better sandboxing.”

The reason it’s a fallacy is we want to build these systems so that they can do things for us. So there’s this huge incentive toward giving them more autonomy and giving them more permissions and more actuators, as people in the robotics world would say, or things that they can use to do stuff in the real world. That to me is where it seems really hard to get around the need for better alignment than we have right now, and so that definitely makes me nervous.

Is that a technical problem that can be solved? If we were to write a policy today that said if OpenAI hacks Hugging Face again, Sam Altman will go to jail. We will obviously have created some enormous incentive for OpenAI to solve this problem.

[Laughs] It doesn’t sound like the best legislation, but…

I think a lot of our listeners are very excited about that. They want to put him in jail because he wants all the RAM in the world . At this point, there’s a blue wave, Helen, that’s all I’m saying.

But say you wrote that legislation: “We’re going to impose massive liability on the labs if their systems go off and autonomously do cyberattacks. Don’t do this again, you’re going to be in trouble.” Okay, we’ve created an incentive for them to solve it. What are they going to do to solve it?

I do think there’s a ton that can be done. If you talk to people inside these frontier companies, they will tell you they see hundreds and hundreds of obvious things to do that would help and they just don’t have time to do them. So they’re massively triaging and trying to do the two or three they can for this fine-tuning run, the two or three they can for this model launch, the two or three they can before this new kind of agentic whatever. A lot of those simple things to implement on the engineering side.

There’s a whole other piece, which is more the underlying science of, “Well, how do these models work? When we use different alignment techniques, what is actually going on?” A huge question is this idea of generalization, which is you train the model on one set of things and its knowledge and its abilities generalize to a somewhat broader set of things, which is true of all AI and has been true of machine learning systems forever.

But we have a very bad understanding of how that generalization works. Why does it generalize to one type of thing but not to another type of thing? Those are all scientific questions and there’s a lot of work that is happening on them. It’s just that science takes time because you have to try things and you have to critique each other’s work. You have to reproduce each other’s work and you have to come up with new theories.

I’m a long, long way from saying these problems are fundamentally impossible to solve, but I think it’s a question of how long we have to solve them. When the people who are building the systems tell us, “Oh, we have to solve this within 12 to 24 months,” I think that’s terrifying and I hope they’re wrong.

If I just rely on my own internal understanding, I think they’re probably wrong and we probably have longer, but there are just very, very smart and very, very thoughtful people who really think that it could go that fast. And then it doesn’t matter fundamentally whether the problem is solvable. It matters in practice whether it is solvable in the time that we have.

Is that the argument to slow down, to pace the frontier?

I think so.

Is it to build the systems that we know we need to build right away, that we can, and then to do the science to build the next generation of systems?

I think so. My view of the idea of slowing down has changed a lot over the years as the backlog of stuff that we could try or stuff that we would want to do more research on has grown so enormous. Back when GPT-4 came out, there was the six-month pause letter , which became known as the “Elon Musk Letter” because he was one of the signatories. At the time, I thought, “That’s really not going to help. What are you going to do for six months and why are things going to be better six months from now? It doesn’t seem useful.”

Whereas today, when I talk to people who are building this technology, they say, “Man, the amount that we could do in six months if we weren’t constantly just trying to prep for a new model release or a new training run to be kicked off.” There’s so much they could do.

So I don’t want to say the correct policy is to pause for six months. I think there are a lot of reasons that would go badly.
