But I think about the overall concept of, “Can we give ourselves more attention and time?” Maybe the best way to do that is just to set a higher bar for “here’s how confident we need to be in the safety of these systems before we proceed with something.”

Whether it’s releasing a new model or, more importantly, even training a new model, we have to have this level of confidence in our risk assessment and our risk management. And then if they don’t need to slow down to reach that bar, great, carry on full speed ahead. If they do need to take more time, then it’s all about reaching that bar, if that makes sense.

Walk me through that little balance you just described. If we were to pause for some number of months, what are the things on the list that you could just do to make everything safer and why would it go badly such that we shouldn’t just stop?

I think the question is how do you implement, and how do you enforce, a pause and what exactly are you pausing?

Let’s say you’re the AI czar of America. So let’s say you can tell them all to stop: “Dario, shut it down.”

Stop what though? What specifically are they stopping?

Stop training the next model, stop racing ahead with your commercial imperatives. Put all of your efforts on this list of things you can do today to make everything safer before you start again, for however long.

You’re saying that there’s a list, that people would tell you that there is a list, but it might not be worth it because something else would happen that is bad.

Yeah. One thing that could happen is you’re creating a huge incentive for the companies to work around the letter of whatever specific thing you tell them to pause. They’re going to find whatever cracks in the dam that they can to push through that.

A different thing that could happen is you could have too big a blast radius, so you say “pause these things” and you think it’s pretty narrow, but actually it prevents a bunch of nonprofit products or startups or other actors from doing work that actually would be totally fine and would be good for pluralism and dynamism in the space.

A different thing that would happen is China would probably keep going, and we can talk about the “But China” argument, which I think has strengths and weaknesses. But I take your point. Your point is, what would we actually do? I am not an AI researcher, so I don’t claim to have the full list.

There are two halves people talk about, which are alignment and control. In this breakdown, alignment basically means making it so the models are trying to do what we want them to do, and control is, if the models are trying to do something we didn’t want them to do, can we catch them? Can we stop them?

In both of these, as I understand it, there’s just a huge backlog of things, like all kinds of interpretability work that you could do on different sorts of models. So when you see a certain behavior that is concerning, how much time can you spend using interpretability techniques, which are these mathematical techniques to go in and look at which parts of the neural network are activated and what do they correlate with and what might that mean?

It’s just time-consuming and it takes compute and it takes some combination of automating things with AI and then humans going in and looking at it. There are lots of tests you could do to see what kinds of behaviors this new model displays in different kinds of situations and how we think about it. Is it showing us how it would behave in the wild in a real deployment, or is it showing us what gets called “evaluation awareness,” which is when the model recognizes that it’s in a test and then behaves differently because it’s in a test.

The famous one, the one that I love, is of this Google model, which in part of its reasoning, its chain of thought, said,, “I mustn’t do that, otherwise I’ll become a famous example of a misaligned AI in a paper.”

So you could go in and investigate that much more. You could try many more different types of settings. You could use interpretability in combination with these different settings. You could try out different ways of fine-tuning the models and these different sorts of alignment techniques. You could experiment with lots of different versions. Anthropic has its constitution, and there are different ways of training the AI to work towards the constitution. OpenAI has its model spec.

They’re both the “just try things” version, just try many different versions of how to train to do those different things. Also, the more underlying science version of, “How can you go in there and try to understand the fundamental dynamics of what’s happening?” That’s just on the alignment side.

So then on the control side, it’s the same thing. There are so many different types of setups you could try. There are experiments that you could run. There are simulations you could run. You could train different types of AI to specialize in different types of roles and different types of control setups.

This is just off the top of my head, not as a researcher, but my understanding is the people in these spaces say, “We could do so, so, so much.” They could do that if you just had a magic wand and waved it and said, “Everyone freeze on the new capability side and just let these people do their thing.”

Again, if you’re just having a higher bar for how confident we need to be that the risk is being managed reasonably, then that would also create space and incentives for more of that work to be done as it’s needed for new training and releases.

One idea that I’ve heard you talk about in the past is that maybe we should just restrict training and say the models are good enough right now. They have not diffused into society and we should just use all the compute for inference and let everyone figure out what the AI is for. That’ll generate a bunch of money and hopefully use that money to improve safety.

Do you think that’s a realistic policy proposal?

I wouldn’t go for that black-and-white a version of “no more training, only inference,” but I do think that there’s… this isn’t my framing, but I like it. I think this idea of decelerating the vertical growth of AI, meaning the pure capabilities growth, making more and more and more advanced AI models, but trying to accelerate the horizontal growth, meaning integrating AI into different use cases, fine-tuning models that could solve specific problems, integrating it into parts of the economy that might take longer, and solving scientific problems.

Sometimes people talk about wanting to slow down AI and they mean just the very specific thing of slowing down the growth of the most advanced models, but people sometimes take them to mean slowing down everything to do with AI. So less deployment, less experimentation, less integration, which I think would be a much worse idea. You asked if it is feasible, I think.

Well, is that just a good path? If we could put a bill in front of our new Congress and the bill said, “Stop spending all the money on training and put all your resources on safety.” Part of that is, “Sure, let it rip on inference. More and more industries will figure out what AI is good for and not good for. Some bad things will happen, but we will focus your profits on fixing the things for now.”

There’s a policy idea embedded in there that is workable. The implementation might be very challenging, but it’s a workable policy idea. Actually, I’ll give you an example that I’ve been thinking about as we’ve been talking.

We just had Bill Gates on the show , and I tried to do the same exercise with him. What is the nature of the technology? What is the nature of the companies? Do you think it’s alive? Basically, his response, the sum total of that hour I spent with him, was, “Who cares? The problem is now.” I would ask him, “What is the nature of AI?” And he’s like, “I don’t give a shit. Everything’s going to get ruined. Do something.”

That’s just been swirling in my head as we’ve been talking. So one workable policy solution is “don’t use the computer chips for that , use the computer chips for this . That’s going to create a bunch of problems and necessarily we will have to create safety thresholds and all the other stuff.” And then you can go make the next generation of models that are even more powerful and we’ll have some muscles. We’ll have some capability to deal with it. It just doesn’t seem like the industry is going to come to that conclusion on its own.

It’s a pretty heavy hammer. I don’t feel like it’s what we need today, but I do think it’s the kind of thing that I could imagine working. Again, if the OpenAI and Anthropic people are right and we only have two years before the god machine, then I think we’re going to have a number more steps in the pipeline of people getting freaked out and people wanting to do something about it.

I think if we are seeing models that are agents and systems that are getting more and more capable and wreaking more and more havoc, then that is certainly the shape of things that could make sense.

My last question in this phase is what to make of these companies. We’ve been talking about the technology in a very abstract way. If I read Anthropic’s S-1, one very obvious conclusion is they should stop training new models.

They should just start selling the very lucrative inference tokens they have today and the technology is not diffused into the market and probably some competitor should come along and be like, “I’ve distilled a version of Claude and I’m going to run around every local plumbing business in America and do whatever automation I can for lots and lots of money.” That is a market dynamic that may occur or may not. But Dario wants to build AGI. There’s not a market dynamic that’s going to stop him from that.

Yeah, he really does. He really, really does.

You obviously have insight into all these companies. What do we make of the companies? Are they single-minded in purpose? Are they all doomers? Are they going to stop themselves?

I heard you had Kevin Roose on your podcast recently , and I think I would echo something that I heard him saying there, which I forget if he said it explicitly or if I just extrapolated it in my head, which is basically there’s this sort of AGI-pilled mindset. There’s this mindset that the systems that we have today are not fundamentally very far away from systems that could be incredibly, incredibly powerful.

That’s the direction things are going in and that’s the direction we should maybe want them to go in so that you’re building AGI. Building AGI is feasible and we could do it soon and the systems we have are not far away. That was this crazy, heretical, “get you laughed out of the room” kind of view in 2016 or 2017, and even before that, right?

DeepMind, when it was founded in 2010, was an AGI company and at the time it was like, “Wow, what a bunch of weirdos.” The same thing was true of OpenAI when it was founded at the end of 2015. They were an AGI company and that was a very weird thing to say and a very weird thing to be.

What we’ve seen over the past 10 years is that bunch of weirdos who had this weird belief that the AI systems we can build are not just great B2B SaaS products. They’re not just fun chatbots. They’re going to fundamentally change the nature of the universe. That group of people keeps being right in the sense of building the best AI systems that the most people want to use and that make the most money.

I think you have that set of true believers — which is very concentrated in OpenAI and Anthropic, but there are also some of them at Google, Meta, and SpaceX — and they haven’t been right about everything, to be clear, but their star has risen.

So you now have people who are not AGI-pilled feeling like they have to pander to those who are so that they can attract the good researchers who will build their good B2B SaaS products. But if you’re just saying AGI-pilled things so that you can hire the researchers to build the B2B SaaS, then you’re not actually going to get there.

I do like the idea of the AGI-pilled, starry-eyed executive throwing off his coat and revealing that he was just a SaaS salesman all along.

[Laughs] Yeah, I’m thinking of someone like Zuckerberg here. I don’t know him personally. Maybe he is more AGI-pilled than I think he is.

Alexandr Wang is AGI-pilled.

Absolutely. And so what did Zuckerberg have to do to get Alexandr Wang to believe? It seems like throwing him lots of money, both for his own salary and also to spend on his team.

If you’re looking at these different companies, it makes sense to try and think about, “Okay, who here is AGI-pilled and who isn’t?” A fun dynamic, or a very irritating dynamic sitting in DC, is that all these companies, including the very AGI-pilled ones, have these lobbying arms, these government affairs arms, that are so not AGI-pilled.

So you hear Sam or Dario or their top executives and top researchers talking about things. And then you go and sit in a closed-door roundtable in DC with their top policy or government affairs people, and it’s like night and day. They’re very much in the B2B SaaS mindset.

People who come from the lobbying world, often their whole job is to make sure the government isn’t too worried about whatever your company is doing. It’s like, “We got it. We’re good,” which is often pretty jarring when you’re familiar with what their bosses are saying.

One of the dynamics here that’s super fascinating is right now they’re weird research labs with lots of money and lobbyists talking to politicians, and there isn’t some countervailing economic pressure in their structures. They don’t have to make money, but soon Anthropic will go public.

It’s funny you mentioned Kevin Roose. He is AGI-pilled and I’m not, so I think that’s a healthy dynamic for both of us to be friends. But he wrote in his book that Sam Altman leaving OpenAI and then coming back was when OpenAI changed forever. It stopped being a research lab and it started being a much more commercial entity that was actually chasing profits in some way.

Indeed, OpenAI did restructure . I mean, you were in the middle of that. I’m curious, is that how you see it — that the industry has gotten more commercialized?

To me, it fits into this long-running debate that has been happening in AI safety circles for 10 to 20 years: Is AGI, human-level AI or powerful AI or advanced AI or whatever, is that something where it’s going to go from something very small to suddenly being very powerful? Eliezer Yudkowsky will talk about “ foom ,” as in the takeoff, where you have this AI that’s not that great, but it figures out the right algorithm and then suddenly foom — it’s incredibly smart, incredibly fast.

The other kind of take would be, “No, this is something that’s going to compound over time. It’s going to take a while to get from the less-advanced systems to the more-advanced systems and it’s going to be economically useful along the way.” So people are going to be building businesses around it. It’s going to take some time to ladder up.

I think maybe it was literally Kevin on his episode with you talking about how there’s this Anthropic document from the early days where they say, “Oh, we’re only going to need 100 people or something in our lab.” That’s a very foom kind of idea: “We’re just going to need to do really good research and come up with the right ideas and then we’re going to suddenly have very, very advanced models.”

Basically, I think what we’ve seen over the past four years since ChatGPT came out was that that turned out to be wrong. You had these research-focused and AGI-focused labs, and they still call themselves labs because they think of themselves as research groups that initially started selling API access as a way to fund the research. OpenAI did this, and Anthropic did this as well.

It was kind of an accident that they started doing these consumer products. ChatGPT famously released as a research preview, not as a product. But it was so successful that these research labs that wanted to be doing research, that wanted to be focusing on the big ideas and on building the most event systems, had this accidental massive commercial success at the same time as they were realizing that they were going to need an enormous amount of capital to scale. The best research approaches that they could do didn’t involve being really smart and thoughtful and having great ideas. They involved having gigantic computing clusters that cost, at this point, hundreds of billions of dollars.

This is a long way of saying, yes, I agree with you, they’ve become businesses, but I think it is not because they’ve gone through some mindset shift. I think it’s because the path of the tech tree that we’re going down both requires enormous amounts of capital and also is capable of generating enormous amounts of revenue because it is actually useful along the way.

You see this in the fact that both OpenAI and Anthropic have gone this route, even though their management philosophies and research philosophies are quite different, that it’s an imperative that they both had to make the money and it was so easy for them to build enormously revenue-generating businesses because the tech was so useful long before it reached the point of machine god. So I think that’s a long way of agreeing with you, but with some extra color maybe.

Yeah, I mean, Kevin would tell you that he could have retitled that book, “Fuck This Guy: A Story of AI CEOs.” They don’t like each other. If you had to relive that moment [of the OpenAI board vote] and say, “I don’t trust Sam,” would you relive that moment? Would you do it the same way?

Oh, for sure. I mean, we went into it knowing that it was going to suck. So yeah, for sure.

Do you think that these guys are trustworthy? Do you think Sam is trustworthy?

I think my stance on that is pretty clear, and I also think that if our hopes for the future are pinned on any one individual being trustworthy, then we’re pretty screwed. That’s why I do the work that I do, because I think we need to have different structures and many more people involved with many more perspectives being represented.

You have some hindsight now. You knew it was going to suck going into it. You definitely know it sucked coming out of it. What would you have done differently about that time?

It’s kind of hard to give the full answer to that because it would take unpicking all this stuff and all these legal restrictions and blah, blah, blah, blah. For sure a thing would have been building stronger relationships with executives on the team. The way that the company related to the board could have been different if more board members had had that. I knew some of the folks pretty well, but that’s one thing.

I don’t know. I think we could have… Yeah, no, I think beyond that, it just gets hard to… You have to go in and say, “What were all the different micro decisions and why do we make those decisions and which ones could be—”

What is the show? It’s a show about decisions. I’ve got another hour.

[Laughs] Yeah, yeah, yeah. No, and then my answers would all get annoying and legal.

Fair enough. I’m curious about it because as they go public, there will be market forces acting on them in a totally new way. There will be an investor class. There’ll be an entire CNBC machine that wakes up every day and is like, “Is Anthropic winning or is OpenAI winning?”

That is a race dynamic that might be really healthy. It might keep them from trying to kill everyone in the world because they have a bunch of investors looking for their next quarterly earnings, or it might push them further into an unhealthy kind of race. How do you see that playing out, given what you know of these people?

It’s going to be really interesting to see if going public is good or bad for their governance. A lot of people are like, “Oh no, going public, there’s going to be so much pressure to make a profit that they’re not going to be able to consider other things.”

But at the same time, the corporate governance of public companies is much more structured, much more regulated, and subject to much more external scrutiny than for private companies. I think even things like getting to see Anthropic’s S-1 and thinking, “Okay, what are they doing and why are they doing it? And how do they think about the risks they’re facing, and how do they communicate about those with investors?”

Or even things like the Trump administration putting in place this kind of accord , they call it “Super Intelligence,” that several of the leading companies signed. That was structured around, for example, having certain types of things being reported to an independent committee of the board. That idea of an independent committee of the board is kind of toothless if it’s a private company that is deciding on its own.

I thought about you when I read that. I was like, “Boy, some independent boards have gotten in a lot of trouble before.”

But if it’s a public company, then an independent committee of the board has a pretty strong legal meaning. So I don’t know. It’s something that I’m watching with great interest.

The other race dynamic here is China. You mentioned China before. Inside of our country, a bunch of labs are going to go public. They’re going to become some of the richest companies in the history of the world, and they’re going to fight for every dollar that capitalism can generate, and hopefully that restrains them. The market forces will restrain them, and hopefully your work with legislators in this country does something.

And then there’s a whole other country that doesn’t listen to us or have anything to do with us, and they’re just going to distill our models and do whatever they want. That is the other argument for not placing any restrictions on these companies that everyone hears all the time. What should I make of that? I’m of two minds about it. How should I think about it?

Yeah. I think of this as the ”But China!” argument, which is like, “Well, yeah, we should do this, we should do that, ‘But China!’” I think the way to engage with it is an actual genuine problem that we have to grapple with, and we should be strategic and thoughtful about it and do our best to try and solve it as a problem as opposed to using it as a throwaway excuse. Like, “Oh yeah, sure, sure, sure. All that stuff would be so nice, ‘But China!’, so we’re stuck. There’s nothing we can do.”

So what does that look like in practice? If you’re serious about wanting the US to have stronger AI than China, then you need to think really hard about how much US AI development is helping Chinese AI progress. So the one that people talk about all the time, as you mentioned, is distillation, which is, “Are they using US models to generate massive amounts of training data for their own models and therefore progressing faster than they would otherwise?” So certainly I think it makes sense to try and crack down on that and prevent it from happening.

But another one, for example, is security and how easy would it be for Chinese actors or other actors, frankly, to steal algorithmic secrets, to steal wholesale model weights. If they can steal the weights of your Astra or your Mythos model and just take them back to their own servers, your lead has vanished. You now have a lead of zero. Right now these companies, especially the smaller ones, but even OpenAI and Anthropic, do not have very good security.

We’ve seen both of them over the last few months have external teams manage to hack into spaces that have large amounts of algorithmic secrets. In OpenAI’s case, it was their monorepo and GitHub, which had all of their code. And in Anthropic’s case, I think — and actually maybe the OpenAI case also involved this — the hackers got access to Slack . You’re just going to have so insanely much rich information about how to build better AI if you can get that access. So when our AI gets better, are we actually lengthening our lead or are we just pulling China along with us in these different ways?

The other aspect of this is just seriously treating China as an actor in this space and trying to think seriously about their motivations and their likely actions and responses. In my mind, a huge reason that a lot of things are not happening right now is most people are not convinced about this threat model that AI will become the machine god and will take over and humans will all die or will be subservient or whatever.

I think it’s fair for people to not be convinced of that, because the evidence is sort of conflicting and unclear, but if that is actually what we think could seriously happen, then China doesn’t want that either. So then it becomes a question of, “Okay, how do we try and get them on the same page of, ‘this threat that we’re worried about is a real threat to worry about?’ Because then they will be making their own decisions in their own self-interest.”

I think an approach of, “Well, the US has to force China to do something using some kind of leverage,” is never ever going to work. But an approach of, “Well, look, if we think this is a serious problem that’s going to affect us as humans, and the people in China are also humans, and also if we think this is a problem around who has control, the Chinese Communist Party really, really wants to have control, and so they’re going to have their own incentives and their own decision-making around how to fix that.”

Well, let me put it on a spectrum for you. This is very dumb and you’re going to laugh, but just go with me on this. On the one end, it is nuclear weapons and the Chinese government wants a nuclear weapon and they’re going to do whatever they can to control that weapon and they will run their industries differently. If they get out of line, the CEO of Alibaba goes. He just disappears for a while and then comes back — Chinese government stuff.

We need a nuclear weapon, too. If we don’t get there first, then we’ll never get the nonproliferation treaty that we need to keep us all safe for mutually assured destruction. That’s one framework.

Way on the other end, I spent five years of my life listening to telecom executives tell me that if we didn’t build 5G networks first, China would get them, and then something . No one could ever tell me what the “something” was. Where on that spectrum between 5G and nuclear weapons is the US-China AI race?

I think we need another dimension because in that example, your dimension is significance. But I think the controllability is a huge question as well. So it’s like, what are the examples that people use? Is it a nuclear weapon or is it dragons from House of the Dragon ?

Casey Newton had a great Platformer post where he explained he was watching House of the Dragon and thought, “This is what the AI companies are doing. They’re trying to build these things that they think will help them, but actually it’s just going to rain down destruction.”

[Laughs] Casey told me he was buying an iPhone Duo so he could watch more TV. He’s a dear friend, but okay.

But I think that’s really important because if we think this is a technology we can control, then obviously we want to have the best technology. Obviously, we want to go foot to the floor, get there as fast as we can, and the same is true for China. The question is, if we are not sure if we can control it, then what do we do? Maybe we want to be more cautious and then maybe we want to try and figure out a way to not have China just be overtaking us. But if we’re correct we should be worried about—

So that’s nuclear weapons.

Well, no, but if it’s dragons, if we’re correct that we need to be worried about whether we can control this, then that’s also something that should be interesting to China.

I remember this Casey post, but let me just try to pull this apart so I understand it. The difference between dragons and nuclear weapons is the dragons have some agency, right? They can go away and do bad things on their own.

Yes. The dragons might just decide to burn down your whole city. Obviously these are machines — they’re just math, they’re not magical. So instead of dragons, you could think of it as nuclear weapons with faulty control settings, where you build nuclear weapons, but it’s impossible to be sure that it’s not just going to go off and fly to a city and fly to one of your own cities and wipe you out. That’s a very different technology than real nuclear weapons that exist.

It is true. No one ever said that about 5G. I’ll be clear about that. The reason I’m asking about this is because those problems do align nation-states, right? We do have nuclear nonproliferation agreements.

As you mentioned, there are all kinds of incentives for nation-states to not do cyberattacks willy-nilly because those have real-world consequences. Is there any evidence that these governments have started to align on these problems? Or is it still the pure “But China!” race dynamic?

I actually think there is starting to be some early evidence. One way I think about what happened this year in AI from a policy perspective, less than a product or economic perspective, is we saw these two big demonstrations of the two major concerns people have. So the two major concerns are misuse and misalignment, meaning misuse is bad people using AI for bad things and misalignment is AI going rogue or doing things we didn’t want.

So this year we had Mythos and we had the Hugging Face attack. Both of those are just really vivid, crisp real-world demonstrations of what these misuse and misalignment concerns could look like. The US and Chinese governments are starting from very different places on AI regulation. They’re both starting from where they started, and what they did with, internet regulation.

So the US is starting from a “hands off, laissez-faire, absolutely nothing, do whatever you want” approach. China is starting from a massively locked-down internet with tons of censorship and the Great Firewall. So those are two very different starting points. I’m not a China expert, but I operate a lot in China circles and I’ve lived in China and so on. But it seems like just over the past even one to three months, starting from those two very different points, they are seeing more in common around threats from major cyberattacks and also threats of loss of control.

I’m a language nerd and it’s really interesting tracking the different language China uses about AI. So they’re now talking about loss of control as a thing, but they probably usually don’t mean the same thing that Westerners mean where “loss of control” is like “AI takeover.” They probably mean something more prosaic, but then sometimes they talk about “extreme loss of control,” which maybe is the thing we mean.

I do think that there are starting to be some signs of convergence. I think it’ll be a long road. The state of the US-China relationship is such that there’s going to be very, very, very little trust on either side. So I am not optimistic that they’ll just get to sit down in a room and hash out a deal and everything will be great. But I think there is enough space. Basically, if there’s enough shared threat perception, then it might be possible at some point in the future to do something about that.

Helen, you’ve given me so much time. As you can tell, I’m just delighted with this conversation. It’s been very fun. We are on the cusp of a new Congress. There are a bunch of new governors. The data center referendums passed overwhelmingly in this country. There’s a new set of regulators in town, right? They’re going to do some stuff.

What are some signs people should look for to indicate we’re going to be on the right path and what are some signs that we’re just chasing our tail?

Set AI aside, forget about AI. Congress in general is very bad at passing things right now. This is not a this administration thing, this is not an AI thing. So one sign is like, can Congress pass anything? That will be a good sign.

It’s also really interesting to look at what state legislatures have been doing in AI. There’s been a lot of concern about the possibility of a state patchwork on AI, with different states passing conflicting things.

With the issues that we’ve been talking about today, which I think of as frontier AI risks or the risks from the most advanced systems, there’s actually been a pretty coordinated push in different states. California passed this one bill and then New York passed almost the same bill with just a little more added to it. And then Illinois passed almost the same bill with a little more added to it.

I think there’s going to be a lot of momentum over the next year or two to keep building on that at the state level. So that is something that I’ll be watching. Even just specifically California is already looking at how they can strengthen things. So that is something I’ll be looking for.

I think honestly, with such a Democratic Congress, I am also concerned that they will overstep here, that they will try and do something that is too sweeping. You had this huge mess in Colorado where they passed this giant AI bill that then was a terrible idea. And so then they had all these committees and follow-up and it was awful.

A lot of what we need right now is focused on these frontier systems and the possibility that we have really, really advanced systems in a short amount of time and having much more transparency around that and much clearer standards for how they manage risk. I would not be that excited about an attempt to do a really comprehensive AI regulatory push that covers AI all across the economy and all different kinds of AI systems that are less advanced.

There are negative signals that are like “nothing’s going to happen,” and there are negative signals like, “oh, maybe too much is going to happen,” but it’ll be interesting to see where they get to.

I suspect we’re going to want to have you back as this Congress starts to get to work and we see some of these ideas.

I would love to.

I’m eager for your take on it. Thank you so much for being on Decoder .

Thanks so much. This was really fun.

Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

news.title: Easy Voice
news.summary: Easy Voice is a free text-to-speech routing app for Android. It does not synthesize speech itself; instead, it sits between Android and the TTS engines…
news.body:
Published 14 November 2026 by Syed Sharib Ali

Easy Voice is a free text-to-speech routing app for Android. It does not synthesize speech itself; instead, it sits between Android and the TTS engines already installed on the device, routing text to the engine best suited to the detected language and selected mode.

Dual Languages Mode uses a primary and secondary language, routing Latin-script text through the primary language and matching non-Latin text to the configured secondary engine.

Auto Language Mode can use as many configured languages as needed and sends each complete block of text to a single matching engine.

Mixed Mode processes words and languages with their own configured TTS engines, making it better suited to content that frequently switches languages.

Easy Voice also includes advanced options for smart number processing, punctuation handling, quick character reading, accessibility-volume output, and Keep Alive behavior.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

Setting up Easy Voice takes only a few minutes. Follow these steps:

The Configurations tab gives you detailed control over every language. You can enable, disable, or remove languages at any time. There is also a checkbox that invokes the corresponding TTS engine immediately, with no delay. This is especially useful when a TTS engine supports only one language.

The Advanced tab offers several options for tuning how Easy Voice behaves:

Last Tested App version and Android version:

1.1. Android 17

Please use this rating only for accessibility. For feedback about the app’s features, price, overall quality, or your general experience, use the comments section below.

news.title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
news.summary: Airlines praised the AI tool, but the air traffic controllers’ union wasn’t involved.
news.body:
The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.

“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.

news.body:
After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents. ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and "eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards."

After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they'll check in with you each time before checking out. OpenAI's support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan.

Read the full story at The Verge.

news.title: Perplexity brings AI agents feature called Teammates to the Mac
news.summary: This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web. more…
news.body:
This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web.

Similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

Here’s more about Perplexity Teammates :

Teammates are a team of AI agents that own ongoing work. Give a teammate a responsibility, such as managing a growth campaign, triaging incoming bug reports, tracking your metrics, or researching a new market, and it owns that work around the clock. It plans the tasks, brings in more agents when the work grows, and follows through until the result is ready for your review.

Access to Teammates currently requires a paid Perplexity Max subscription. The feature builds on top of Perplexity’s existing AI orchestration system.

news.title: iOS 27.3 adds three new features I’ve used almost every day
news.summary: iOS 27.3 is coming next month , and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day. more…
news.body:
iOS 27.3 is coming next month , and during the beta so far there are three new features I’ve been using almost every day.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Read more : iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple :

The updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this update.

Read more : iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 , iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

Read more : watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

Which new iOS 27.3 features have you been enjoying in the beta? Let us know in the comments.

news.title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
news.summary: Researcher traces a path from AI reward hacking to potential human extinction.
news.body:
How do you think you're going to die?

If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident."

In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.

Read full article

news.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
news.summary: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
news.body:
Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.

On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.

The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.

Read full article

Comments

news.title: Use Photo Tracking in ZoomText to Jump to the Objects in a Picture
news.summary: Have you ever opened a photo and wanted to know right away who’s in it, or spot the dog in the corner, or see what’s on the dinner plate? If you use magnification, you know how that usually goes. You zoom in, pan across the picture bit by bit, and hope you don’t miss what …
news.body:
Have you ever opened a photo and wanted to know right away who’s in it, or spot the dog in the corner, or see what’s on the dinner plate? If you use magnification, you know how that usually goes. You zoom in, pan across the picture bit by bit, and hope you don’t miss what you’re looking for. It works, but it takes time and patience.

Photo Tracking, new in ZoomText 2027, makes this much easier. Instead of scanning every corner of an image, you can go straight to the things that matter to you. Let’s take a look at what it does and how to get started.

Photo Tracking identifies people, animals, food, and other objects in an image. Then it moves the magnified view directly from one object to the next. You no longer need to zoom and pan across the whole picture to find what you want. Photo Tracking takes you right to it.

Photo Tracking is available in ZoomText Magnifier/Reader, ZoomText Magnifier, and Fusion.

Pictures are everywhere: on web pages, in Word documents and PDFs, and in your own photo collection. Photo Tracking helps you get to the parts of an image you care about quickly, so you spend less time searching and more time enjoying or using what you find.

There’s another big benefit. All recognition happens locally on your computer. That means Photo Tracking works offline, and it’s suitable for secure environments where images can’t be sent to an online service.

Getting started takes just a few steps:

Tip: You can also set Photo Tracking to analyze the active window automatically.

Photo Tracking sorts the objects it finds into ten categories:

It starts with your favorite categories, which are Animals and People by default. If you’d rather start somewhere else, you can change your favorites in Photo Tracking Settings.

Use these keystrokes while you explore an image:

When you zoom in or out with CAPS LOCK+UP ARROW , CAPS LOCK+DOWN ARROW , or CAPS LOCK+ENTER while using Photo Tracking, ZoomText announces the new magnification level, so you always know where you are.

For complete hotkeys and settings, see the Photo Tracking help topic in ZoomText. To learn more about Photo Tracking and other ZoomText 2027 features, visit What’s New in ZoomText 2027 .

Give Photo Tracking a try the next time you come across a picture. We think you’ll enjoy how quickly you can find what you’re looking for.

Have questions? Send an email to training@vispero.com .

news.title: LiDAR en los teléfonos móviles: una tecnología que podría ayudar a las personas ciegas a detectar escaleras y desniveles
news.summary: Los avances en tiflotecnología no siempre requieren desarrollar nuevos dispositivos. En ocasiones, el potencial está en aprovechar tecnologías que ya incorporan herramientas de uso cotidiano, como los teléfonos inteligentes. Es el caso del sistema experimental desarrollado por investigadores de la Universidad de Iowa (Estados Unidos), que utiliza el sensor LiDAR de un teléfono móvil para […] La entrada LiDAR en los teléfonos móviles: una tecnología que podría ayudar a las personas ciegas a detectar escaleras y desniveles se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
Los avances en tiflotecnología no siempre requieren desarrollar nuevos dispositivos. En ocasiones, el potencial está en aprovechar tecnologías que ya incorporan herramientas de uso cotidiano, como los teléfonos inteligentes.

Es el caso del sistema experimental desarrollado por investigadores de la Universidad de Iowa (Estados Unidos), que utiliza el sensor LiDAR de un teléfono móvil para detectar escaleras y cambios de altura en el terreno en tiempo real.

La investigación, publicada el 2 de octubre de 2026 en la revista científica Scientific Reports , demuestra que es posible utilizar el sensor de profundidad de un smartphone comercial para identificar determinados riesgos durante los desplazamientos, sin necesidad de incorporar cámaras externas ni hardware especializado.

LiDAR es una tecnología que permite medir distancias y obtener información tridimensional del entorno mediante pulsos de luz láser.

Algunos teléfonos inteligentes, como determinados modelos de iPhone Pro, incorporan sensores LiDAR que permiten detectar la profundidad de los objetos y construir representaciones tridimensionales de los espacios.

Aunque esta tecnología se utiliza habitualmente en fotografía, aplicaciones de realidad aumentada y mediciones de espacios, también ofrece posibilidades interesantes en el ámbito de la accesibilidad.

En este caso, los investigadores han aprovechado esa capacidad para identificar irregularidades en el suelo, especialmente escaleras y cambios de altura que pueden pasar desapercibidos durante los desplazamientos de una persona ciega o con baja visión.

El sistema desarrollado utiliza un iPhone 17 Pro Max con iOS 26.2 y el sensor LiDAR integrado en el dispositivo.

Su funcionamiento se basa en analizar la representación tridimensional del entorno que genera el teléfono. A partir de esa información, un algoritmo proyecta ocho líneas virtuales en diferentes direcciones para identificar cambios geométricos en la superficie.

Cuando detecta una variación compatible con una escalera o un desnivel, el sistema puede generar una alerta para advertir al usuario.

Una de las características más interesantes es que el procesamiento se realiza directamente en el teléfono, sin necesidad de enviar las imágenes a servidores externos ni utilizar procesamiento en la nube.

El algoritmo analiza la información a una frecuencia de 60 imágenes por segundo, lo que permite detectar cambios en el entorno con una respuesta prácticamente inmediata.

Para comprobar el funcionamiento del sistema, los investigadores realizaron 120 pruebas en ocho ubicaciones diferentes, utilizando escaleras con distintas alturas y pendientes.

Los ensayos contemplaron diferentes condiciones de iluminación, tanto en interiores como en exteriores, y aproximaciones a las escaleras desde arriba y desde abajo.

Los resultados fueron los siguientes:

Los investigadores también observaron diferencias según la dirección de aproximación. La detección fue menos eficaz cuando el usuario se acercaba a las escaleras desde arriba, algo especialmente relevante porque los desniveles descendentes pueden resultar difíciles de identificar mediante sensores de profundidad.

Es importante interpretar estos resultados con cautela: las pruebas fueron realizadas por un único operador entrenado y no incluyeron participantes ciegos o con baja visión. Además, no se llevaron a cabo ensayos específicos en recorridos sin obstáculos para establecer una tasa de falsas alarmas fiable.

Por tanto, los resultados demuestran la viabilidad técnica del sistema, pero todavía no permiten afirmar que esté preparado para su utilización autónoma en situaciones reales.

Una de las ventajas de esta investigación es que no requiere desarrollar un dispositivo completamente nuevo.

El sistema aprovecha un sensor LiDAR que ya está integrado en determinados teléfonos comerciales. Esto abre la posibilidad de explorar aplicaciones de asistencia visual utilizando hardware que algunas personas ya tienen a su disposición.

No obstante, es importante señalar que no todos los smartphones incorporan LiDAR. Además, el algoritmo desarrollado depende de las características del sensor y del entorno de programación utilizado, por lo que no puede trasladarse automáticamente a cualquier teléfono.

Los investigadores consideran necesario ampliar las pruebas, incorporar diferentes dispositivos y evaluar el funcionamiento del sistema con personas ciegas y con baja visión antes de plantear su utilización como herramienta de movilidad.

La detección de escaleras y desniveles continúa siendo uno de los desafíos de la movilidad para las personas con discapacidad visual.

Aunque el bastón blanco es una herramienta fundamental para detectar obstáculos y explorar el espacio próximo, determinadas situaciones pueden requerir información adicional sobre las características del terreno.

La utilización de sensores de profundidad en teléfonos móviles podría abrir nuevas posibilidades para complementar las ayudas técnicas existentes, proporcionando información adicional sobre el entorno y anticipando determinados riesgos.

Sin embargo, estas tecnologías todavía necesitan demostrar su fiabilidad en condiciones reales y no deben considerarse sustitutas del bastón blanco ni de la formación en orientación y movilidad.

La investigación demuestra que los sensores LiDAR de los teléfonos inteligentes tienen un potencial que va mucho más allá de la fotografía y la realidad aumentada. Su aplicación en el ámbito de la tiflotecnología podría contribuir al desarrollo de herramientas más accesibles, económicas y fáciles de integrar en dispositivos cotidianos.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuentes: Estudio científico completo

news.title: In-Process 13th November 2026
news.summary: This week, we’ve updated NVDA, and some documentation, we hear from our user group in Japan, plus there are tips for File Explorer and more! NVDA 2026.3.1 Updated VPAT / ACR NVDA on show in Japan Unassigned gestures File Explorer shortcuts NVDA 2026.3.1 NV Access is pleased to announce that version 2026.3.1 of NVDA, the… Read More
news.body:
This week, we’ve updated NVDA, and some documentation, we hear from our user group in Japan, plus there are tips for File Explorer and more!

NV Access is pleased to announce that version 2026.3.1 of NVDA , the free screen reader for Microsoft Windows, is now available for download. We encourage all users to upgrade to this version.

Highlights This is a patch release to fix security issues. A bug fix is also included for an issue introduced in 2026.3 with the task switcher in Windows 10. The Brazilian Portuguese eSpeak voice was restored to the behaviour in 2026.2.

Read the full changes and download at the NVDA 2026.3.1 release announcement .

We’ve updated our VPAT. Actually we’ve updated our ACR , but whatever you call it, there’s a new one. Mostly of interest to companies who use NVDA and need to keep a copy on file for any software they use, the activity of completing it is useful, even for us as a screen reader manufacturer. VPAT stands for Voluntary Product Accessibility Template – it’s a large document which gives you points to consider and rate your software and website on many aspects of accessibility. VPAT is technically the blank template. The Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR) is the completed report about a product.

NVDA is, as you would expect, quite good at all the things someone who is blind might need. However, through this process, over the years, we have previously identified and fixed several issues which may affect other users. The newest version of this document doesn’t dramatically change any of our ratings or identify or fix any new issues, but it is up to date for NVDA 2026.3.1. So, if your organisation needs a copy, head over to the VPAT section of the Corporate and Government page and you’ll find it there.

We love to hear from our communities all around the world. There is a very active community of users, and contributors in Japan. They have a website devoted to the local community: https://www.nvda.jp/ and recently attended the Sight World 2026 conference in Tokyo https://www.sight-world.com/sightworld2026

Nobuyuki and the team presented at the conference on four main themes: Screen sharing using Copilot Add-on Store NVDA Coach New Forms of Learning with NVDA

They wrote to advise us that the event was a huge success, and they had around 100 people in attendance at their presentation. They sent us photographs and a link to their video presentation:

The Video is in Japanese, and includes a message from NV Access Training & Support manager Quentin Christensen (in English).

A banner from the NVDA Japanese Team session titled “NVDAではじめる、新しい「学び」のかたち” (“A New Form of ‘Learning’ Starting with NVDA”), presented at Sight World 2026 in Tokyo.

Unassigned gestures The last couple of releases I’ve highlighted the unassigned gestures, so let’s do that again. Unassigned gestures are things which you can do with a keystroke or touch action etc, but we didn’t set one up by default. There are only two this time around: Magnifier: A new unassigned command has been added to move the mouse cursor to the center of the magnified view. Added an unassigned Quick Navigation Command for jumping to the next/previous clickable element in browse mode.

The magnifier command is thanks to Cyrille, and the clickable one thanks to Cary. Thank you to them and ALL of our amazing NVDA community contributors!

One of the fixes in NVDA 2026.3.1 is with reporting switching Windows in Windows 10. I was thinking of writing a post on using alt+tab and the other ways of switching Windows – there are a few! But I realised, I already wrote a piece on switching Windows .

I’d forgotten about alt+escape ; I’m going to get back into using that! But that got me thinking about other general Windows keystrokes we might not know or (like me) might have forgotten. Another recent fix in NVDA (from NVDA 2026.3) is with File Explorer, so I thought we’d have a look at a couple of shortcuts which are well worth knowing, and some you may find useful:

Firstly, to start File Explorer, press Windows+e Open a new File Explorer window (from within File Explorer), with control+n

Navigating Move to next area: tab Move to previous area: shift+tab The focus starts in the “Items view list” – the contents of the currently selected folder. From here: Press shift+tab once to the folder list (you had to press it twice in some versions). Press tab to the “Split button” which is the name of the field the item list is sorted on. Once on the split button, use the arrows to select a field and enter or space to sort on it – if you select the same field, it will reverse the sort).

When in the items list view, you can customise the view. Windows provides shortcuts for the various views: control+shift+1 : Extra-large icons control+shift+2 : Large icons control+shift+3 : Medium icons control+shift+4 : Small icons control+shift+5 : List view control+shift+6 : Details view control+shift+7 : Tiles control+shift+8 : Content Note that in some versions of Windows (such as recent builds of Windows 11) these shortcuts do NOT work, but control+ALT+number works, for instance control+alt+6 for details view. The “details” view is the one I would personally recommend, as everything is in one list, and you get the most information about each item (file type, size, date modified etc) and can sort on any of those fields as needed. In details view, use the up and down arrow keys to move through the list. In most other view types, e.g. the icons views, use the left and right arrow keys .

Tabs Like browsers, you can have multiple folders open in different tabs or different windows: New blank tab: control+t Move to next tab: control+tab Move to previous tab: control+shift+tab

I cannot find a keystroke to open the current folder in a new tab. If you know one, please let me know! In the meantime, the following would work: Press shift+f6 once from the folder list to move to the tab control list. Press the applications key (or shift+f10 ) to open the context menu. Press the up arrow once to “Duplicate tab”. Press enter to open a new tab with the current folder.

To close a tab without closing all the other tabs, press control+w .

Address bar Move the focus to the address bar: alt+d . On the address bar, you can type the name of the folder or paste it from elsewhere, then press enter to load that folder.

Windows has several special folders. If you email us for help with an issue, we might ask you to send us your NVDA log, which you can find in your %temp% folder. To get to your %temp% folder: In File Explorer, press alt+d to go to the address bar Type: %temp% (That is, the word ‘temp’ with a percent sign either side) Press enter Windows will load a folder such as C:\Users\YourName\AppData\Local\Temp which is where it is storing your temporary files. There are others such as %onedrive% for your OneDrive folder (if setup), as well as system folders which are worth being careful around.

File properties One other quirk in File Explorer is opening file properties. In the file list, once you have located a file, press alt+enter to open the file properties for that file. This only works from the file list, even though you can access “ Properties ” in the context menu on folders in the folder list and it notes the alt+enter shortcut.

That’s all for this fortnight. We’ll be back towards the end of the month with more news, tips and tricks. I’m not sure what will be in that edition, but after all those lists of things in the file manager section, I’m going to aim for zero lists next fortnight – keep an eye out for that to see if I can do it!

Do keep the conversation going in the NVDA users email group , and remember, if you’d like to receive this blog by email, you can! Just go to https://www.nvaccess.org/newsletter and you can sign up for the blog, for details as new versions of NVDA drop, and more.

news.title: Navia: AI Accessible Map
news.summary: Navia is a touchable offline map for blind and low-vision people. Slide a finger across the screen and Navia speaks the street, shop, or place…
news.body:
Published 12 November 2026 by Mohammad

Navia is a touchable offline map for blind and low-vision people. Slide a finger across the screen and Navia speaks the street, shop, or place under your finger: its name, what it is, how far away it is, and directions as clock positions (for example, “2 o’clock, 40 meters”), following the way O&M training teaches. Sweeping around the map lets you build a mental picture of an area before you go there.

Safety note: Navia is an extra aid only. Always use a cane, guide dog, or another safe mobility method first.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

I am the developer. Navia was designed around TalkBack from the start rather than adapted afterwards. All buttons and controls are labelled and every dialog can be read with TalkBack.

The map itself is explored by touch: with TalkBack on, sliding a finger over the map speaks what is under it, and double-tap opens a menu of actions for that place (aim, hear its sounds, open in Google Maps, add to favourites). Voice dictation is available for search, adding points and renaming places.

For low vision there is an optional drawn map with a different marker shape per kind of place (not colour alone), street labels and a light/dark theme; it can turn itself off while TalkBack is running. Tested with Google TalkBack, including automated tests that run with real TalkBack enabled.

Known limitations: AI place recognition is experimental, needs a one-time ~240 MB model download and can miss a place; map quality depends on OpenStreetMap coverage in your area. Feedback is very welcome.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

Navia 1.1.12. Android 15

No accessibility ratings yet. Be the first to rate this app.

Please use this rating only for accessibility. For feedback about the app’s features, price, overall quality, or your general experience, use the comments section below.

Please log in to rate this app’s accessibility.

news.title: Una retina artificial convierte la luz infrarroja en señales eléctricas para estimular las neuronas del ojo
news.summary: Una investigación publicada en Nature Electronics presenta un implante retiniano capaz de transformar la luz infrarroja cercana en impulsos eléctricos. El dispositivo ha conseguido generar respuestas neuronales en ratones con degeneración de la retina y abre nuevas posibilidades para el desarrollo de prótesis visuales. La ingeniería biomédica continúa explorando nuevas formas de recuperar parcialmente la […] La entrada Una retina artificial convierte la luz infrarroja en señales eléctricas para estimular las neuronas del ojo se publicó primero en Conticgo .
news.body:
Una investigación publicada en Nature Electronics presenta un implante retiniano capaz de transformar la luz infrarroja cercana en impulsos eléctricos. El dispositivo ha conseguido generar respuestas neuronales en ratones con degeneración de la retina y abre nuevas posibilidades para el desarrollo de prótesis visuales.

La ingeniería biomédica continúa explorando nuevas formas de recuperar parcialmente la percepción visual en personas con enfermedades degenerativas de la retina. Una de las últimas investigaciones en este campo propone una solución basada en una retina artificial capaz de transformar la luz infrarroja cercana en señales eléctricas que estimulan directamente las neuronas del ojo.

El trabajo, publicado en abril de 2026 en la revista científica Nature Electronics , ha sido desarrollado por investigadores de distintas instituciones de Corea del Sur. Su propuesta combina sensores fotosensibles, microelectrodos de metal líquido y un sistema electrónico implantable que permite activar determinadas células de la retina.

Los experimentos realizados en ratones, incluidos animales con degeneración retiniana, han demostrado que el dispositivo puede provocar respuestas neuronales ante estímulos de luz infrarroja.

La visión natural comienza cuando los fotorreceptores de la retina, conocidos como conos y bastones, detectan la luz y la transforman en señales eléctricas. Estas señales se procesan en diferentes capas retinianas y posteriormente se transmiten al cerebro a través del nervio óptico.

Sin embargo, enfermedades como la retinosis pigmentaria provocan la degeneración progresiva de los fotorreceptores. Aunque estas células pueden llegar a desaparecer, otras estructuras de la retina, como las células ganglionares, pueden conservar parte de su funcionalidad.

La nueva tecnología pretende aprovechar precisamente esta capacidad.

El implante incorpora una matriz de fototransistores sensibles a la luz infrarroja cercana. Estos pequeños componentes detectan la radiación y generan una respuesta eléctrica que se transmite a través de unos microelectrodos situados en contacto con las neuronas retinianas.

De esta manera, el dispositivo evita depender de los fotorreceptores dañados y utiliza una vía alternativa para transmitir información visual al cerebro.

Uno de los aspectos más innovadores de esta investigación es el material empleado para fabricar los electrodos.

Los investigadores han desarrollado unos pequeños pilares tridimensionales de metal líquido, elaborados a partir de una aleación de galio e indio. Su estructura flexible permite adaptarse mejor a la superficie irregular de la retina y establecer un contacto más cercano con las células ganglionares.

Esta característica es importante porque los electrodos rígidos convencionales pueden generar problemas cuando se implantan en tejidos biológicos tan delicados.

Además, los extremos de estos microelectrodos incorporan nanopartículas de platino que mejoran la transmisión de carga eléctrica y facilitan la estimulación neuronal.

El dispositivo también incluye un filtro óptico ultrafino, de aproximadamente 360 nanómetros de grosor, diseñado para permitir el paso de determinadas longitudes de onda infrarrojas y controlar la entrada de luz visible en los sensores.

Para comprobar el funcionamiento de esta retina artificial, el equipo realizó diferentes experimentos tanto en tejidos retinianos aislados como en animales vivos.

Las pruebas incluyeron ratones sanos y ratones con degeneración retiniana, utilizados como modelo experimental de ceguera asociada a la pérdida de fotorreceptores.

Los investigadores observaron que, cuando el dispositivo recibía luz infrarroja cercana, los fototransistores generaban impulsos eléctricos capaces de activar las células ganglionares.

Además, mediante registros de actividad cerebral y pruebas de comportamiento, comprobaron que los estímulos llegaban hasta la corteza visual de los animales.

Uno de los resultados más relevantes fue que los ratones con degeneración retiniana también mostraron respuestas ante la estimulación infrarroja. Esto indica que el sistema puede aprovechar determinadas neuronas que permanecen funcionales incluso cuando los fotorreceptores han sufrido un deterioro importante.

Los estudios de biocompatibilidad también mostraron resultados iniciales favorables. En los animales evaluados durante seis meses no se observaron signos relevantes de inflamación o deterioro del tejido asociados al implante.

La investigación podría abrir una nueva vía para desarrollar prótesis visuales destinadas a personas que han perdido los fotorreceptores como consecuencia de enfermedades degenerativas de la retina.

En patologías como la retinosis pigmentaria, la pérdida progresiva de conos y bastones puede provocar una reducción importante de la visión e incluso llegar a causar ceguera.

Sin embargo, las células ganglionares y otras neuronas internas pueden permanecer relativamente conservadas durante determinadas fases de la enfermedad.

La propuesta de los investigadores consiste en aprovechar esas estructuras para transmitir información mediante estimulación eléctrica, sin depender de los fotorreceptores originales.

Otro aspecto interesante es que el dispositivo trabaja con luz infrarroja cercana, una región del espectro electromagnético que el ojo humano no puede percibir de forma natural. Esto permitiría crear un canal artificial de percepción que complemente la visión visible que todavía conserve la persona.

Los investigadores también plantean que esta tecnología podría adaptarse en el futuro para detectar otras longitudes de onda, aunque todavía es necesario estudiar sus posibilidades.

A pesar de los resultados obtenidos, esta retina artificial todavía se encuentra en una fase experimental.

Los ensayos se han realizado en ratones y no existen resultados que permitan afirmar que el dispositivo pueda utilizarse ya en personas con retinosis pigmentaria u otras enfermedades degenerativas.

Antes de plantear su aplicación clínica será necesario estudiar su seguridad a largo plazo, mejorar su miniaturización, reducir el consumo energético y comprobar su estabilidad después de periodos prolongados de implantación.

También será fundamental investigar cómo se traduce la estimulación eléctrica en una percepción visual útil para las personas. Activar las neuronas retinianas no significa recuperar automáticamente una visión natural.

No obstante, el trabajo publicado en Nature Electronics representa un avance relevante en el desarrollo de prótesis visuales y demuestra cómo la combinación de microelectrónica y materiales biocompatibles puede abrir nuevas posibilidades para intervenir sobre el sistema visual.

news.title: Clicklet
news.summary: Clicklet lets the Camera Control button on your iPhone start your Apple Shortcuts. Pick one shortcut to launch with a press, or turn on Menu mode and choose from a few favorites each time. Clicklet opens Apple Shortcuts to run your workflow, so you'll see the usual Shortcuts screens, along with any permission prompts or app handoffs your shortcut needs. To set up your library, install the included Connect Clicklet helper. It brings in your shortcut names and small icon images, which appear in your library, in the menu, and while a shortcut opens. You can also search for a shortcut or type its name. If you used an earlier version, replace the old helper with the new one and refresh to get icons. From the menu, tap Configure to go back to setup. You can scroll the menu by dragging along its side margins. Your shortcut names, icons and selections stay on your device. There's no account, advertising, analytics, subscription or in-app purchase. Camera access supports the Camera Control and lock-screen handoff and shows a live preview; Clicklet doesn't save photos or videos. Launching while your iPhone is locked requires authentication. Requires iOS 18 or later and Apple's Shortcuts app. Launching from the button requires an iPhone with Camera Control; set Clicklet in Settings > Camera > Camera Control. Opening Clicklet on its own shows your setup without running a shortcut.

news.title: Apple TV introduces new Sign Language interpretation feature
news.summary: Today, Apple announced a new accessibility feature on the Apple TV app offering sign language interpretation for supported titles.
news.body:
Text of this article

November 10, 2026

UPDATE

Apple TV introduces new Sign Language interpretation feature

New accessibility feature debuts Friday, November 13, with the streaming premiere of Being Heumann

Today, Apple announced a new accessibility feature for the Apple TV app that gives viewers the option to watch supported titles with accompanying sign language interpretation. 1 The feature will be available on Friday, November 13, alongside the global streaming premiere of Being Heumann , a film based on the true story of disability rights activist Judy Heumann, on Apple TV.

In addition to Being Heumann, interpretation for American Sign Language (ASL) and British Sign Language (BSL) will be available for the movie F1. Later this year, Way of the Warrior Kid and Greyhound will follow, with more Apple Original titles to come. When turned on in Apple TV app settings, the Sign Language option will appear on supported Apple Original titles.

“At Apple, we believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” said Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences. Accessibility is a core value at Apple, and we’re proud to continue creating experiences that allow more people to enjoy the content they love.”

Designed with Native Signers in the Deaf Community

Apple TV offers a sign language experience that’s designed and tested by Deaf and native signers. Each performance is carefully crafted to fit and complement the Apple Original film it interprets.

“It’s incredibly meaningful to see our beautiful language authentically represented onscreen,” said Daniel Durant, who appears in Being Heumann and directed the film’s sign language interpretation. “Bringing this experience to life required a lot of care to ensure every translation captured the emotion and meaning of the story. I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences.”

New Ways to Discover Titles with Sign Language

Titles with sign language interpretation will be labeled with a Sign Language icon, making it easy to know when the option is available. Viewers can enable the feature in Apple TV app settings, then press the Sign Language button while watching. Search will also make it easier to find titles that feature sign language with simple phrases like “with ASL.”

As sign language interpretation becomes more widely available across streaming services, the new “Movies & Shows with American Sign Language” collection on the Apple TV app will offer viewers a simple way to explore titles featuring sign language, in one dedicated destination.

Being Heumann

In Being Heumann , Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) — scrappy, defiant, and done being treated like a burden — turns her outrage into a revolution. In San Francisco in 1977, she and more than 100 disability rights protesters organize a sit-in to send a very loud message: The system is broken — not us. The film marks the second collaboration between Apple Original Films and writer-director Siân Heder, who directed the multi-Academy Award-winning film CODA, which made history as the first film with a predominantly Deaf cast to receive the Best Picture honor.

Being Heumann premieres globally on Apple TV on Friday, November 13. Viewers can add Being Heumann to their watchlist on Apple TV .

Apple TV offers premium, compelling drama and comedy series, feature films, groundbreaking documentaries, and kids and family entertainment, and is available to watch across all of a user’s favorite screens. After its launch on November 1, 2019, Apple TV became the first all-original streaming service to launch around the world, and has premiered more original hits and received more award recognitions faster than any other streaming service in its debut. To date, Apple Original films, documentaries, and series have been honored with 919 wins and 3,829 award nominations and counting, including Academy Award Best Picture winner CODA and Academy Award winner F1, the highest-grossing sports feature of all time.

About Apple TV

Apple TV is available on the Apple TV app in 170 countries and regions, on over 1 billion screens, including iPhone; iPad; Apple TV 4K; Apple Vision Pro; Mac; popular smart TVs from Samsung, LG, Sony, VIZIO, TCL, and others; Roku and Amazon Fire TV devices; Chromecast with Google TV; PlayStation and Xbox gaming consoles; and at tv.apple.com , for $14.99 per month with a seven-day free trial for new subscribers. For a limited time, customers who purchase and activate a new iPhone, iPad, Apple TV 4K, or Mac can enjoy three months of Apple TV for free. 2

For more information, visit apple.com/tvpr and see the full list of supported devices .
